cover.tagline: Word-by-word annotations, every mark measured from the original audio
howto: Start with the map page and read the chapters as one continuous line;
Each chapter opens with a sentence tying it to the last one; the IPA above each word reflects how it was actually said;
Every paragraph ends with a summary, every chapter with questions — answer them before opening the book again.
howto_sections: Skim the symbol table first so you know what each mark means;
Each section opens with a line tying it to the last one; the IPA above each word is how it was actually said;
Every paragraph ends with a summary, every section with questions — answer them before opening the book again.
howto_single: Skim the symbol table first so you know what each mark means;
The IPA above each word is how it was actually pronounced; red marks what was raised;
Read the paragraph summary after each paragraph rather than at the very end.

legend.title: How to read the annotations
rows: The IPA directly above each word is its actual pronunciation here; ˈ primary stress, ˌ secondary.
Prominent words sit higher (H) / level (M) / lower (L) than the sentence, measured from F0.
Pitch movement across the stressed syllable: rising / falling / level.
Semitone offset of each syllable from the sentence median.
The vowel swapped in by reduction; the IPA row shows the reduced form.
Linking: final consonant to initial vowel, or vowel to vowel.
Elision: final /t/ /d/ dropped before a consonant.
Flapping: /t/ /d/ after a voiced sound and before an unstressed vowel.

symbols.title: Symbol table
symbols.caption: Prominence in red, reduction in blue, linking in teal arcs, unreleased and elided sounds in brackets — four families that never overlap.

summary.head: Paragraph summary | reduced {weak} · linked {link} · unreleased {unrel} · elided {elide} · flapped {flap}

chart.title: Reading the pitch numbers
chart.intro: The number above a syllable is its median F0 minus the sentence median, in semitones. Positive is higher than the sentence average, negative is lower.
chart.practice_title: How to practise with this table
tips: Read the word-level H / M / L first, then the syllable numbers, then say it yourself and compare.
Follow the shape, not the absolute value. Within ±1 semitone is measurement noise; ±3 is audible.
High-then-low is a fall, typical of statement endings; low-then-high rises, typical of emphasis.
levels: well above the sentence; usually emotion or emphasis
the peak of this sentence sits on this word
a little above the sentence average
level with the sentence; not perceptually prominent
clearly below; often a falling ending
very low; often faster speech or reduction

practice: First pass: read only the English for meaning. Skip the IPA or your attention fragments.
Second pass: say only the red words — those are what the speaker lifted. Get them right and the sentence frame follows.
Third pass: hum the syllable numbers as a melody, then fit the English into it.
Finally look at the teal arcs and brackets: linking and elision come from speed, not memorisation.
